items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I played with Kenny Clarke with one of my -- he was on my first recording session, Here’s Comes Frank Foster, done in 1954. I played with him on a couple of other subsequent recordings.

ctx.x: What did being a bebopper mean?

Being a bebopper meant that you concerned yourself with certain elements of the music, like melody and chord changes, especially the chord changes, and rhythms where instead of the [Foster sings a repetitive drum pattern], the heavy four associated with the swing era, you had [Foster sings a widely varied rhythm], drummers dropping bombs. That became the expression used for the way drummers, Max Roach and Kenny Clarke, et cetera played. We liked the idea of playing with drummers who dropped bombs instead of…

items.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995
items.q: Ed Thigpen, yes, and of course Kenny Clarke, the late Kenny Clarke, the late Leo Wright who played with Dizzy, and there were some great musicians who got jobs in the studio.

ctx.x: Ed Thigpen, yes, and of course Kenny Clarke, the late Kenny Clarke, the late Leo Wright who played with Dizzy, and there were some great musicians who got jobs in the studio. Herb Geller, an alto saxophonist, white American, he went over there and so did Sal Nistico.
